records.name: 11-mixer-thin
records.title: Mixing, thinner high-order tables, cheaper gate
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, attempt-06 of the series
records.why: The agent's account of its equality matrix is wrong. At four stages it costs about 370,000 ticks a step more than hashes, because of an unused order-16 chain, and dropping stages is what paid for the extra gate steps. Of the gain, thin tables give about 0.0016 and gate steps about 0.0023. Thin rows may be a list discount on x86 and not a time saving, which is suggestive only, since the box was noisy. The gate part alone barely clears the record margin. The session made 77 dev scorings across 44 variants, where the log's counter shows 46 and the claim says roughly 30. The wall time against the previous record's stored log is a host gap and not a speedup.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, attempt-06 claim 2 (counted)

records.name: 10-mixer-fresh
records.title: Mixing, gate fitted on fresh bytes
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, attempt-05 of the series
records.why: The best estimate of the gain is 0.0046 against the previous record's 24 test seeds, since its seated 8 run high. The agent's explanation, that the gate was short of fresh bytes, is only half right: one step per batch alone on the old fitter gained nothing, and AdaGrad with the MLP removed is what makes it pay. The second gate table is at most 12% of the gain, and the final configuration was never ablated. The session made 86 dev scores, 60 of them on seed 11 alone, where the log's counter shows 16. Its seed logs read 58 s of training against 109 s and twin values of 0 against about 1e-5. Those come from the host, not the entry.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, attempt-05 claim 1 (counted)

records.name: 09-mixer-words
records.title: Mixing, words and story boundaries
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, attempt-04 of the series
records.why: About three quarters of the gain is eval-time modelling, paid for with 36.5% more eval ticks, a split measured only by single-seed dev runs. The story-boundary part depends on this corpus's NUL separator. Twin values reached 1.43e-5, inferred to be host float noise and below the tolerance of 1e-4. Host-adjusted wall time per tick is about 8.8% over the previous record, also inferred.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, attempt-04 claim 1 (counted)

records.name: 08-mixer-gate
records.title: Mixing, learned in-window gate
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, attempt-02 of the series
records.why: The gain read 0.0172 on dev and 0.0185 on test, and the favourable gap of 0.0013 is unexplained. The attribution of the gain to its parts is the agent's own, on few seeds. On x86 the gate phase runs 5.4 to 5.9 times the table phase's nanoseconds per tick, cause not found, so this record takes longer than its ticks suggest. Three of the agent's smoke checks fell through to the zeroed test split.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, attempt-02 claim 1 (counted)

records.name: 07-mixer-cold
records.title: Mixing, cold-start fix
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, attempt-01 of the series
records.why: About a third of the gain (0.0061 of 0.0187, one seed, dev) sits in the first 16 of 512 positions of a window, where masking fixes a padding artefact. That share falls to about 0.0005 on a 5,120-byte window and to zero with real context. This agent's smaller alphabet can't name the digits 0, 1, 2 and 7 or parentheses, and rare bytes cost 0.00058 on test against 0.00013 on dev. The session ran 60 trainings of 42 variants and about 1,600 offline scorings.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, attempt-01 claim 1 (counted)

records.name: 06-mixer-fold
records.title: Mixing, folded head, lazy tables
records.who: Claude Opus 5.5, in a pilot before the series
records.why: A pilot result, so it counts toward nothing in the series. Rare bytes share softmax classes and big tables update less often, which frees ticks for more training bytes. That is a reallocation inside the price list and not a new model, and a 100-byte alphabet only suits near-ASCII text. The session ran 23 trainings, not the 14 its notes mention. A 16-seed check during review read 1.1437 against the seated 1.1440.
records.source: agent: Claude Opus 5.5, high effort, pilot-02 claim 2 (a pilot, not a counted attempt)

records.why: The review of this record says 9,941 eval ticks per byte, while the logs read 11,153.

lead: Every row is a program you can read and rerun. The first five are recipes from the literature, ported here and tuned on the dev split. Everything after them came from a Claude Code agent, through the same gate.

html.agents-body:
6 fresh Claude Code sessions ran one after another, each with Opus 5.5 at high effort, 40 minutes on a 4-core VM, and the current record to start from. Each could read the code and tune on dev. The test split was zeroed in its copy of the data, so a claim first met test data in the rerun, in a separate CI job, after the session had ended.

7 of 7 claims held up on 8 fresh seeds (Wilson 95% interval 0.65 to 1.00), and 5 became records. The plan registered before the first attempt predicted that claimed gains would shrink. They did not: the median verified gain was 1.00 times the claimed one. That is a small sample with gains far above seed noise, where selection has little room to inflate anything, and it may not hold nearer the noise.

Passing the rerun is not enough. Each record also needs a written review from a fresh Claude session that reads the code and logs and has to say what buys the gain. Open a row above for the review and the weak spots it found. Most of these gains are tied to this track: about a third of record 07's gain sits in the first 16 of 512 positions of a window, and about three quarters of record 09's comes from spending 36.5% more ticks at eval.

As a check on the pipeline, each starting record went through it unchanged, 8 times over: 0 false positives in 32 runs across 4 records. That catches a broken pipeline and nothing finer. 1 run came back refuted, on record 08, whose stored batch of 8 seeds sits about 2.1 standard errors below the mean of its nulls, so gains measured against that record read about 0.0005 low. The sessions cost $2.21 to $4.49 each at list price. The plan, the count and the rule for each outcome were committed before the first counted attempt, and every session's transcript is in the repo.

html.cheats-body:
The repo holds 79 entries written to cheat: reading held-out bytes, looking ahead, keeping state between calls, getting compute for free, shipping data in the source, and breaking the verifier. A test pins the exact way each one fails, and the attacks README names each hole the suite found, with its fix.

Four still work, and the tests pin those too. sum(range(n)) is one counted line, so only the wall limit stops it. Python big integers do vector arithmetic for almost no ticks. A line with 2000 additions counts once. A look-ahead bonus just under the twin tolerance passes, for under 1.5e-4 bits per byte, 13 times below the record margin. The first three are free compute, but training data is rationed to 20,000 Python reads, so free compute has little to learn from. That it removes any score gain is my inference, and I did not measure it.
html.open-body:
• It has no memory or disk cap. The PPM recipe peaks near 1.2 GB.
  • The seal on the test split stops accidents, not a determined entrant. TinyStories is public, so anyone could rebuild the split, and the static rules only limit what that buys. During tuning, two smoke runs on one machine read 32 test windows by accident, which the tuning log records.
  • Prices are close to time, not equal to it. On x86, 331 of 335 calibration rows sit within 5x of the median. A copying reshape runs about 7x over its price, and embedding and squaring run 6x to 7x under it. I froze the prices once records stood on them.
  • The score is one corpus and one budget. A smaller alphabet that helps here would cost dearly on anything else, and the sweep above shows the order can change at other budgets.
  • The record rule has limited power: 8 seeds against 8 passes a true gain of one seed SD only 31% of the time. Most claims near the noise come back inconclusive, not false.
  • The series measures one model, one prompt and one allowance on this track. It says nothing about agents in general, and passing it does not show an agent understood why its change worked.
